title: Looking back: the streams
hook: many streams and places, one Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the code: a personal side and a panth side, kept one practice at a time. Your line was the way. Did you keep your one practice a second time? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

If you could stand in one Sikh place for a single hour, which would it be? Nankana Sahib, where tradition places Guru Nanak's birth. Kartarpur, where tradition says he farmed in his last years. Anandpur, where the Khalsa began. Hemkunt, up among snow and a cold lake. Or somewhere much closer: the gurdwara a short drive away, with folding tables stacked against the wall for langar. This year walked through those places, and through the many streams of Sikh life that gather in them. Today we look back at the streams and the places together, and at what runs through all of them.
screen: `ONE PLACE, ONE HOUR.` → `NANKANA, KARTARPUR, ANANDPUR, HEMKUNT.` → `OR THE GURDWARA DOWN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the streams differ, and that's real. The Udasis kept a life of renunciation. The Nirmalas gave themselves to learning. The Nihangs keep their blue and their old ways of speech. The Namdharis wear white. There are Sindhi devotees of Nanak, Sikh families in Assam, communities shaped by craft and trade, and Sikhs in the West who came to the path as adults. Different dress, different tunes, different emphases. Looking back, nobody had to pretend those differences away. Second, places hold memory. A gurdwara often stands where something happened: a birth, a field worked, a stand taken, a death. Sikhs travel to them to remember, and to sit where the Gurus' story touched the ground. Third, and this is the thread. Walk into one of those halls at dawn, and watch what happens. Someone lifts the cloths from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the day begins with its word, in the same Gurmukhi letters. The snow is different, the language of the street is different, the food in the langar is different. The book at the center is the one we have been reading all year. Fourth, the Granth gives a line for walking between streams. Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I have come to get along with everyone. That's a fair way to visit another sangat. Not to rank it, not to correct it, but to sit down, cover your head, and listen. Many streams, many places. And in the gurdwaras we visited this year, one Guru open at the center.
screen: `THE STREAMS REALLY DIFFER.` · `PLACES HOLD MEMORY.` · `THE SAME GRANTH OPENED AT DAWN.` · `NO ONE A STRANGER.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a place you'd visit. Settle, and breathe. Choose one place from this year, or a gurdwara near where you live. Let it come into view. The door. Shoes off, head covered, hands washed. The hall, and the Granth under its canopy. Now ask what you'd do first. Sit and listen to kirtan? Bow? Help in the langar, washing plates? Stay there for a while, in your mind, doing that one thing. If you pray, you can carry a prayer in with you. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Today, at the streams and the places: real differences, real memories, and the same Granth opened at the center. Today's word.
Your line: many streams. Today, look up one gurdwara near you, its hours or its langar, and keep it in mind as a place you might one day walk into. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs from many streams travel to historic gurdwaras to remember the Gurus' lives, and in gurdwaras near and far the day begins with the Guru Granth Sahib opened and read.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the gathering that sits together before the Guru's word, wherever it meets.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs are all one group who do everything the same way.
what it means: the panth holds many streams and places, with real differences, and the Granth at the center of them.
what a scholar hears: orders, schools and communities, each with its own emphasis, and Guru Arjan's line for meeting them: no one a stranger.

notes: Look-back day. Day 1361 (the streams close) listed the whole block and used the Japji's rivers-and-ocean image; this day takes a different angle (what differs, what places hold, what is the same) and uses Guru Arjan's 'no one a stranger' line.
Please confirm Ang 1299 for 'na ko bairee nahee bigaanaa, sagal sang ham kau ban aaee' and the paraphrase.

The Namdhari community holds a distinct view of a continuing line of living Gurus; the script avoids saying every stream holds 'one Guru' in the same sense, and says 'in the gurdwaras we visited this year, one Guru open at the center'. Please check this is fair.
